First reasoned review: 52f8fbe615d1 / de8e4550241c / c5bfdf67d34e

Method
Read RULES.md and TAXONOMY.md. Ran atomscan --mode slow --follow=none and
cleave facts on each original file. Used Ghidra native decompilation, Rizin,
pefile, dnfile/dncil IL decoding, Pillow image extraction and OpenSSL AES
resource decoding. No specimen code was executed. Reports, decompiled code,
extracted payloads and original/final scan JSON are in the session scratch
review-52-de8-c5 directory. The supplied Triage and Bazaar pages were not
accessible through the web tool; their labels were not used as proof.

52f8fbe615d1: MALICIOUS; multi-exploit Windows mining worm/loader
The original PE is a large native bundle, not an NSIS installer. Embedded
OpenSSL/PHP, WinPcap, mining and exploitation components explain many names.
The scanner's NSIS-named embedded units often include the remaining bundle
as trailing data; their reported sizes are not the real PE extents.
At 0040ed1a, code passes explicit net-stop, sc-config-disable and netsh
firewall-off command strings to 00448c40. The latter calls CreateProcessA,
sets the child window hidden, optionally waits, then closes the handles.
The caller 0040c889 runs this teardown path. It targets WinDefend, MpsSvc,
SharedAccess and wuauserv, rather than merely mentioning these services.
At 00433592, code constructs target-IP-specific SMB exploitation commands
using --InConfig, --DaveProxyPort, --TargetPort 445, --DllPayload and
--DllOrdinal options. It launches architecture-specific DLL payload handoffs
into the target process via the same command runner. These are active exploit
launch paths, not passive embedded documentation. The bundle also has mining
protocol templates, mining configuration, competing-miner handling and tools
including Mimikatz. Defender/firewall teardown and the remote exploit path
tip the verdict; a mining login template alone would not.
No deployment authorization or live target history was supplied. Exact
malware family is unresolved; the collector's long family-name list is not
an identification. Isolated PE extents at 0x7c313, 0x9dc71 and 0x2d2e1b scan
without hostile findings. Their library code must not inherit the trailing
worm's service commands as their own behavior.

de8e4550241c: MALICIOUS; bitmap-concealed managed payload loader
The file claims a PDF previewer in version information but its entry point
constructs SteamLaundry.LaundryForm. InitializeComponent at RVA 4250 obtains
resource OPlus, constructs ChannelHarvester with limit 64512 and reads RGB
channels in column order. The recovered bytes form a valid managed PE.
The same method resolves AppDomain.Load via "L" + "oad" and VB LateGet,
then selects a type/method and dispatches through VB LateCall with Invoke.
The first extracted assembly is HWMonitor / a Sokoban UI with SmartAssembly
control-flow and delegate/string obfuscation. Its constructor reaches Justy.
Justy converts resource/key arguments from hex, obtains IDGl from the outer
assembly, crops the image by 177 columns and 225 rows, reads column-ordered
little-endian ARGB values, reads a length prefix, and XOR-decodes the bytes.
Mist uses a key derived from the last byte XOR 112 and BigEndianUnicode key
bytes, wrapping at the key string's character length (three bytes here).
This recovers another valid managed PE, Noogen.Validation. The second-stage
loader loads it in AppDomain and dispatches a method by type/method indexes.
The third stage is heavily obfuscated and contains a native PE-mapping /
remote-context manipulation routine and a further encrypted resource.
The local evidence establishes the concealed multistage activation and
unrelated UI/version claims. It does not establish the final C2 or confirm
the supplied njRAT family label; neither is asserted by a new trait.
Concealment plus managed activation and deceptive packaging tip the verdict.

c5bfdf67d34e: MALICIOUS; StormAttack resource-DLL injector
Native banners identify StormAttack. Configuration at VA 00404120 is 3,
which selects Active Setup installation in 00401cb0. At 00401900 the code
creates an HKLM Active Setup component under a generated GUID, writes a
REG_EXPAND_SZ StubPath containing a self-copy path, copies and patches its
own image (mode becomes 4), and launches that copy. Mode 4 extracts DLL
resource 101 and invokes the injection helper 00401150. That helper creates
iexplore/notepad/calc according to configuration, allocates remote memory,
writes the DLL path, resolves LoadLibraryA, and calls CreateRemoteThread.
00401390 builds COMSPEC /c del of the current module's short path and
launches cleanup. A separate mode-1 path replaces LanmanServer's ServiceDLL;
the finding correctly describes present code, not execution in mode 3.
Service-install mode is also present. Resource 101 is a 39936-byte PE DLL.
The surviving installer/injector and self-delete paths justify the verdict;
no live DDoS target or successful injection is claimed. Existing four hostile
traits already cover these behaviors accurately and were retained.

Trait changes
Moved neutral HTTP HEAD/TLD, AES-name, debugger-event and service-command
observations to their proper capability homes. Removed standalone Shellcode
family attribution and unsigned-system-name masquerade inference; retained
individual process-name observations. Removed mining-template/pool-only
hostile composites; mining protocol observations remain notable. Updated
consumers, including the njRAT native Defender-stop consumer.
Bound firewall teardown to SharedAccess stop and startup-disable commands,
rather than unrelated service actions anywhere beside its name. Native
Defender, firewall, mining and SMB command evidence is limited to mapped
sections (section:any) to exclude appended unrelated payload bytes.
Added mining-plus-Defender-teardown and SMB-DLL-exploit-plus-Defender-teardown
hostile combinations. They describe file-scoped evidence, not a YAML-proven
data flow or runtime success. Deduplicated the broad bitmap dispatch finding
when the more specific VB dispatch finding is present.

Controls
build_controls.py creates six inert PE fixtures: their entry point returns;
they do not call their imports. check_controls.py checks mapped evidence,
missing exploit fragments, overlay-only evidence, unrelated service actions,
mining-only behavior and ordinary debugging. They test matchers, not malware
execution. Scope and semantic corrections intentionally change detection
populations; ordinary mining/debugging and loose name-only attribution must
not preserve the former convictions. No sample-specific filename, hash,
endpoint or size exception was added.

Final checks before validation
All six focused controls passed. Final atomscan scans retained four local
hostile traits on the mining worm, two on the bitmap loader, and four on the
StormAttack injector. All three original SHA-256 values matched the queue.
Each original has exactly one .MALICIOUS marker, with a one-line reason of
at most 72 characters.
